segments.text: Episode fifty-five. Next stop... the runaway Moon.
The Moon looks like it's always been there, and always will be. But it's slowly leaving us.
segments.headline: It's leaving

segments.text: Every year, the Moon moves about three point eight centimeters farther from Earth. About as fast as your fingernails grow.
How do we know so precisely? Apollo astronauts left mirrors on the Moon.
segments.headline: Mirrors on the Moon

segments.text: Observatories on Earth fire lasers at those mirrors and time how long the light takes to come back. About two and a half seconds.
segments.headline: Lasers and mirrors

segments.text: Why is it drifting? Tides. The Moon pulls Earth's oceans into bulges, and Earth's spin drags those bulges slightly ahead.
segments.headline: Blame the tides

segments.text: The bulges pull the Moon forward, flinging it a little outward. And they act like a brake on Earth's spin.
segments.headline: A cosmic brake

segments.text: So our days are getting longer. Hundreds of millions of years ago, a day lasted only about twenty-one hours.
Will the Moon escape? No. Long before that could happen, in billions of years, our Sun will change everything.
segments.headline: Will it escape? No
